title: The Ollie and the Street
bigQuestion: How did one no-hands trick change where and how people skate?

story.title: No Hands
story.kicker: At a Florida skatepark in the late 1970s, a board leaps into the air and nobody is holding it.
paragraphs: It is the late 1970s at a concrete skatepark in Florida. A young skater sits on the edge of a bowl, watching. Every rider who flies above the coping does the same thing. They reach down, grab the board with one hand, and hold it so it does not fall away. Everyone thinks that is the only way to get air.

Then an older rider drops into the bowl. He carves fast across the bottom and rolls up the far wall. Near the top, his back foot stamps down on the tail. The board pops up off the wall. His hands stay out by his sides, not on the board. For a moment, rider and board hang above the coping together.

The young skater leans forward. How is the board staying under his feet? Nothing is holding it. The rider turns in the air and comes back down onto the wall, wheels first, and rolls away. Someone at the edge shouts. Another skater tries it on the next run and the board shoots off on its own.

Riders in Florida were trying this trick in the late 1970s. One of them, Alan Gelfand, had the nickname Ollie, and the trick took his name. Within a few years, a teenager named Rodney Mullen would do it on flat ground. Once a board could jump with no hands and no ramp, the whole city became a place to skate.
story.think: Why would a trick with no hands be harder to believe than a trick where the skater grabs the board?

lessons.title: Alan Gelfand's No-Hands Air
lessons.mainIdea: In the late 1970s, Alan 'Ollie' Gelfand popped his board into the air on a ramp wall with no hands, and the ollie was named for him.
reading: Alan Gelfand skated in Florida in the late 1970s. His friends called him Ollie. He found that he could pop his board into the air at the top of a transition without grabbing it. At the top of the wall, he stamped hard on the *tail*, the back end of the board that bends upward. The board lifted, and he lifted with it.

Other skaters called the trick the *ollie* air, and later just the ollie. An ollie is a jump where the skater pops the tail and the board rises with their feet, with no hands. At first, the ollie was done only on ramps and in bowls. Many skaters saw it in magazine photos before they ever saw it in person.

The ollie depended on an older idea: the *kicktail*. That is the upturned tail of a board. Larry Stevenson's patent for a kicktail was granted in 1971. Without a tail to push on, there is nothing for the back foot to snap. The kicktail made the kickturn possible, and later it made the ollie possible.

words.d: the back end of a skateboard deck, usually bent upward
a jump where the skater pops the tail and the board rises with the feet, with no hands
an upturned tail on a skateboard deck; Larry Stevenson's patent for it was granted in 1971

lessons.title: How a Board Pops Up
lessons.mainIdea: In an ollie, the back foot snaps the tail, the ground pushes back, the board tips up on its back wheels, and the front foot drags it level.
reading: An ollie is a chain of forces. First, the back foot snaps the tail down hard. The tail hits the ground. By *Newton's third law*, when one thing pushes on another, the second pushes back just as hard in the opposite direction. So the ground pushes up on the tail, and the board starts to rise.

The board also acts as a *lever*. A lever is a stiff bar that turns around a point called a pivot. Here the pivot is the back wheels. When the tail goes down, the nose swings up. The turning effect is called *torque*, found by force times the distance from the pivot. Here is a worked example. A back foot pushes with 500 newtons, 0.15 meters from the back wheels. 500 times 0.15 is 75, so the torque is 75 newton-meters.

Now the board is tilted, nose high. The front foot slides up toward the nose. Grip tape is rough, so friction lets the shoe drag the board upward. The front foot then pushes the nose forward and down until the board is level. The rider jumps at the same time and pulls the knees up, so the board has room to rise.

words.d: when one thing pushes on another, the second pushes back just as hard in the opposite direction
a stiff bar that turns around a fixed point called a pivot
the turning effect of a force, found by force times the distance from the pivot

look.title: A Ruler and a Board
look.text: Lay a ruler on a desk so one end sticks out past the edge. Tap the end that sticks out. The ruler turns at the desk edge, and the far end lifts. Now picture a skateboard. The back wheels are the desk edge. The tail is the end you tap. When the tail is struck, the nose lifts. The longer the distance from pivot to foot, the bigger the turn for the same push.

check.q: When the tail hits the ground in an ollie, what pushes the board up?

check.why: By Newton's third law, the ground pushes back up on the tail as hard as the tail hits it.

check.q: In an ollie, what is the pivot of the lever?
check.why: The board turns around the back wheels, so the nose rises when the tail goes down.

check.q: A foot pushes with 400 newtons, 0.15 meters from the pivot. What is the torque?
check.why: 400 times 0.15 is 60 newton-meters.

lessons.title: How Long an Ollie Lasts
lessons.mainIdea: Hang time depends on how high the rider rises; a 30-centimeter ollie keeps a rider in the air about half a second.
reading: Once a skater leaves the ground, gravity takes over. The skater rises, slows, stops at the top, and falls back. The time from takeoff to landing is called *hang time*. The path of the skater's middle traces a smooth arch called a *parabola*. A higher jump means a longer hang time.

There is a formula for hang time. If h is the jump height, the time is 2 times the square root of 2h divided by g. Here is a worked example for a 0.30-meter ollie. First, 2 times 0.30 is 0.60. Next, 0.60 divided by 9.8 is about 0.061. The square root of 0.061 is about 0.247. Last, 2 times 0.247 is about 0.49. The rider is in the air about half a second.

Half a second is very short. In that time the front foot has to drag the board level and both feet have to come back over the bolts. That is why skaters practice the same motion many times. The landing matters too. Bending the knees on landing spreads the stop over more time, which makes the force on the legs smaller.

words.d: the time a skater spends in the air, from takeoff to landing
the smooth arch-shaped path of something thrown or jumping through the air

check.why: Stopping over a longer time means a smaller force on the legs.

lessons.title: Freestyle Skating
lessons.mainIdea: Freestyle was a style of flat-ground skating done as a routine, and Rodney Mullen became its best-known rider.
reading: In the 1970s and 1980s, one kind of contest needed no ramp at all. It was called *freestyle*. Freestyle skaters did tricks on smooth flat ground, one after another, in a routine set to music. They spun on the back wheels, stood the board on its end, and flipped it with their feet. Judges scored the whole routine.

Rodney Mullen grew up in Florida. As a teenager he won freestyle contests again and again, and he kept inventing new tricks. He rode for Powell Peralta, one of the biggest skateboard companies of the 1980s. Freestyle taught him to control a board with tiny movements of his feet.

Freestyle boards were often smaller and lighter than ramp boards. They had a tail and a nose to stand on and spin. Freestyle contests faded by the end of the 1980s, but the control they built did not. Many of today's flat-ground tricks began as freestyle tricks.

words.d: a style of skating on flat ground, with tricks done one after another in a routine
a planned set of tricks done in order, often to music, for judges

There is no ramp, no rail and no curb, only a board and feet.

lessons.title: The Ollie on Flat Ground
lessons.mainIdea: In the early 1980s, Rodney Mullen did the ollie on flat ground, so a skater could jump with no ramp at all.
reading: Gelfand's ollie happened at the top of a ramp wall. In the early 1980s, Rodney Mullen found a way to do it on *flat ground*, meaning level pavement with no ramp. He snapped the tail, slid his front foot up, and the board rose off the floor with his feet. Skaters had never seen a board jump from flat ground with no hands.

This changed what a skater could do. With a flat-ground ollie, a skater could hop up onto a curb, over a crack or onto a low ledge without stopping. It turned the whole street into terrain. In skating, *terrain* is any surface or object a skater rides, from a bowl wall to a curb.

Learning it still takes many steps. First, a skater practices standing still on grass or carpet, where the board cannot roll away. Next, they try it rolling slowly on smooth, flat ground with a helmet buckled and pads on. Only after many clean landings do they try to ollie up onto something low, such as a painted curb.

words.d: level pavement with no ramp
any surface or object a skater rides, such as a bowl, a bank or a curb

The second crouches as they roll, snaps the tail, slides the front foot, and the board hops up onto the curb with their feet on it. They keep rolling without stopping.

lessons.title: Kickflips and Flip Tricks
lessons.mainIdea: Rodney Mullen invented the kickflip as it is done today, along with other flip tricks like the heelflip and the 360 flip.
reading: Once the board could jump from flat ground, Mullen began to spin and flip it in the air. His best-known invention is the *kickflip* as skaters do it today. In a kickflip, the skater ollies, and the front foot flicks off the toe-side edge of the nose. The board flips over along its long side, then the feet catch it and land.

Skaters had flipped boards in other ways before, but Mullen's version starts from an ollie. He also invented the *heelflip*. In a heelflip, the front foot flicks off the heel-side edge with the heel, and the board flips the other way. Mixing a flip with a spin led to the 360 flip, also credited to Mullen.

A flip trick is called a *flip trick* because the board turns over under the skater. These tricks look like magic, but they follow the same rules as the ollie. They are learned after a steady rolling ollie, first by practicing the flick standing still on grass. Landing with both feet over the bolts is the goal every time.

words.d: an ollie in which the front foot flicks off the toe-side edge of the nose so the board flips along its long side
an ollie in which the front heel flicks off the heel-side edge so the board flips the opposite way from a kickflip
a trick where the board turns over under the skater in the air

The second slides the front foot up and pushes the heel off the heel-side edge. That board rolls over along its long side too, but in the opposite direction. Both boards land wheels down, and both skaters catch with their feet.

check.why: In a kickflip the front foot flicks off the toe-side edge. The heelflip uses the heel side.

check.why: Flip tricks build on the ollie, and the flick is first practiced standing still.

lessons.title: The Bones Brigade
lessons.mainIdea: Powell Peralta's team, the Bones Brigade, gathered young riders such as Tony Hawk and Rodney Mullen in the 1980s.
reading: Powell Peralta was a skateboard company run by George Powell and Stacy Peralta. Peralta had skated with the Zephyr team in the 1970s. In the 1980s he built a team of young riders called the *Bones Brigade*. A skate *team* is a group of skaters a company sponsors to ride its products in contests, photos and videos.

The Bones Brigade included Tony Hawk, Steve Caballero, Mike McGill, Lance Mountain, Tommy Guerrero and Rodney Mullen. Some rode vert ramps, some rode street and one rode freestyle. Tony Hawk joined as a young teenager and became one of the best-known skaters in the world.

The company's boards had bold *graphics*, the pictures printed on the bottom of a deck. Artist Vernon Courtland Johnson drew many of them, often with skulls and bones. Kids could spot a Powell Peralta board across a parking lot. A board's art became a way for a skater to show who they were.

lessons.title: Skate Videos on Tape
lessons.mainIdea: The Bones Brigade Video Show of 1984 showed skaters that tricks could be learned by watching moving pictures at home.
reading: In 1984, Powell Peralta released The Bones Brigade Video Show. It was a skate *video*, a film of skaters doing tricks, sold on tape. Families could play it at home on a VCR, a machine that played video tapes. Skaters watched it over and over.

A photo shows one frozen moment. A video shows the whole trick: the crouch, the pop, the landing. Skaters could pause, rewind and watch the feet. Powell Peralta made more videos, including Future Primitive in 1985 and The Search for Animal Chin in 1987. Videos became one of the main ways tricks spread.

Videos also made skaters famous in towns with no skatepark. A kid in a small town could study the best riders in the world without leaving home. Copies were passed from friend to friend. Later, in the 1990s, videos from many companies would take over this job.

words.d: a recorded film of moving pictures, such as a film of skaters doing tricks
a video cassette recorder; a machine that played video tapes on a TV

lessons.title: Thrasher and TransWorld
lessons.mainIdea: Two magazines that started in the early 1980s, Thrasher (1981) and TransWorld SKATEboarding (1983), kept skating connected after parks closed.
reading: When parks closed and sales fell in the early 1980s, skaters needed ways to stay connected. Two new magazines filled that need. Thrasher began in 1981 in San Francisco. TransWorld SKATEboarding began in 1983. Both covered vert ramps, backyard ramps and the new street skating.

Each *issue*, one printing of a magazine, carried photos, interviews and contest results. Many issues also printed *sequence* photos. A sequence is a row of photos taken quickly, one after another, showing each step of a trick. A skater could study a sequence like a set of instructions.

Magazines linked skaters in different places. A reader in Illinois could see what was happening in California or Florida that month. Ads listed skate shops and mail-order catalogs. For many skaters in the 1980s, the magazine and the video were the closest thing to a skatepark.

words.d: one printing of a magazine, such as the March issue
a row of photos taken quickly, one after another, showing each step of a trick

lessons.title: Backyard Ramps
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1980s, skaters built wooden halfpipes in backyards, and small mini ramps became a common place to learn.
reading: With concrete parks closing, skaters turned to wood. Friends and families built halfpipes in backyards and driveways. The frame was made of wooden ribs cut into a curve. Sheets of plywood were bent over the ribs to make a smooth transition. A metal pipe along the top edge served as coping.

Tall ramps with vert walls were used for big airs and contests. Many backyards had a *mini ramp* instead, a smaller halfpipe with no vertical part. On a mini ramp, a skater can learn to pump, kickturn and roll back and forth at low speed. At the top of each wall is the *platform*, a flat deck where skaters stand and wait their turn.

A safe ramp starts with a strong frame and smooth, tight plywood with no gaps or loose screws. Adults with building experience did, and still should, lead the work. Riders on any ramp wear a buckled helmet and pads. Taking turns on the platform keeps two skaters from crashing at the bottom.

words.d: a small halfpipe with curved walls but no vertical part
the flat area at the top of a ramp wall where skaters stand and wait

lessons.title: Curbs, Ledges and the Street
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1980s, street skaters used the ollie to ride curbs, ledges and banks, starting with low objects first.
reading: By the mid-1980s, the ollie had opened up the street. Skaters such as Mark Gonzales and Natas Kaupas showed new ways to ride things found in towns. A curb could be ollied onto. A *ledge*, a long low block like the edge of a planter, could be ground along. A *bank*, a slanted wall of concrete, worked like a small ramp.

Street skating used what was already there, so anyone with a board could try it. Some skaters in videos also jumped down stairs and rode handrails. Those were advanced feats done by experienced riders, not things to try while learning. Many skaters also met trouble from guards and police, because skating in some public places was banned.

A safe way to start street skating is at a skatepark's street section or on a painted curb in an empty lot, away from cars. First, practice the ollie rolling on flat ground. Next, ollie onto a curb only a few centimeters high. Then add a little height when landing feels easy. A buckled helmet and wrist guards go on every time.

words.d: a long, low block, like the edge of a planter or bench, that skaters ride along
a slanted wall of concrete that works like a small ramp
